h: Shipyards, sewing machines and the canal
p: Kilbowie Road runs through the heart of Clydebank, and the town around the shopping centre has a story that's well worth knowing. This was one of the great shipbuilding towns of the world. The John Brown & Company yard on the Clyde built some of the most famous ships ever launched, including the Queen Mary, the Queen Elizabeth and the QE2. Down by the river, the giant Titan Crane still stands as a reminder of those days.

Clydebank was also home to an enormous Singer sewing machine factory, and the local railway station is still called Singer. In March 1941 the town was devastated by the Clydebank Blitz, when German bombing raids destroyed or damaged most of its homes. The town's resilience is a big part of its identity, and the Clydebank Museum, in the Town Hall, tells these stories along with a remarkable collection of sewing machines.

The Forth and Clyde Canal runs right through the centre, which is why the shopping centre sits on both banks. The towpath makes a good, flat walk or bike ride, and you can follow it in either direction for as long as your legs allow. It's a pleasant way to see a different side of the town.

Getting here is straightforward, with Clydebank and Singer stations nearby and regular buses from Glasgow city centre. If you've got a car, Loch Lomond and the start of the Highlands are only a short drive further west, so the shopping centre makes a handy stop on the way to bigger adventures.
